Patient Vignette: Mrs. E.

Mrs. E. is a 73-year-old, divorced woman who has worked as a forester for the last forty years. She presents for treatment at the urging of her adult daughter, who has grown concerned about her mother's increasing isolation and volatile temper. Mrs. E. is lean, calloused, and direct. She sits with her arms crossed, her gaze fixed on a point just past my left shoulder. She says she is here because her daughter "won't shut up about it," but she does not believe talking will help.

The story she tells begins in the woods behind her childhood home in a rural, northern European village. She was the youngest of five children, born to a father who was a lumberman and a mother who was "tired." When she was four years old, her father began to beat her. She says it was not the kind of punishment the other children received. It was a private, methodical ritual. He would call her into the toolshed, close the door, and use a leather strap he kept hanging on a nail. She learned to count the holes in the leather to distract herself. She learned to stop crying after the third strike, because crying made him angrier. She learned that the smell of sawdust and motor oil meant pain. She never told her mother. She says, "You didn't. You just went out and played in the mud until your legs stopped shaking."

At age twelve, she grew taller and stronger than her father expected. One afternoon, when he raised the strap, she did not flinch. She looked him in the eye. He stopped. He never hit her again, but he never spoke to her directly again, either. She left home at sixteen, married at nineteen, and divorced by twenty-five. She says her husband was a good man, but she could not stand to be touched. She felt a "crawling" sensation on her skin whenever he reached for her in the dark. She began sleeping on the couch. He left. She did not blame him.

She found her way into forestry almost by accident. She took a job with the state park service and discovered that the forest was the only place she felt safe. The trees did not ask questions. The work was physical and solitary. She learned to read the land, to identify disease in a stand of pines, to predict a fire line. For forty years, she has spent ten to twelve hours a day alone in the woods. She says, "The trees don't lie to you. They don't promise you anything and then take it back."

Now, at 73, her body is beginning to fail. Her knees are worn. Her hands ache with arthritis. She cannot walk the long transects she used to. She has been forced into a desk job, managing a small team of younger rangers. She says the office is a "cage." She cannot sit still. She finds herself scanning the room for exits. When a colleague touches her shoulder to get her attention, she flinches so hard she knocks a coffee cup off her desk. She has taken to eating lunch in her truck, alone, with the doors locked.

She sleeps poorly. She wakes three or four times a night, drenched in sweat, certain she has heard her father's footsteps on the gravel. She does not remember the dreams, only the feeling of waiting for the blow. During the day, she is irritable. She has snapped at her daughter for humming. She has told a young ranger to "stop creeping up on me" when he simply walked into the room. She feels a constant, low-grade tension in her shoulders, as if she is bracing for impact.

She avoids her daughter's house because the hallway is dark and narrow. She avoids hardware stores because the smell of oil makes her nauseous. She avoids crowds because she cannot track all the people moving around her. She has stopped going to the grocery store. She orders her food online and has it delivered to the ranger station.

When I ask her what she wants from therapy, she is quiet for a long time. Then she says, "I just want to stop being so tired. I've been waiting for something bad to happen my whole life. It already happened. It happened a long time ago. But my body doesn't know it's over." She looks at me then, directly, for the first time. Her eyes are clear and hard, like chips of flint. "Can you tell my body it's over?"
